extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulemaking officials, agency decisionmakers, environmental advocates and counsel submitting public comments
extracted.subtask_description: A formal public-comment letter urging EPA to remove the unlawful affirmative defense from NESHAPs for oil & gas source categories, grounding the request in statute, case law, prior agency actions, empirical evidence of excess emissions, and environmental justice concerns; asks for prompt, agency-wide removal of the affirmative defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative defense is illegal
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA correctly recognizes the affirmative defense is illegal; removal is required. (See 88 FR 83,899; 'the affirmative defense is illegal.' )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground the rulemaking decision on the statutory prohibition and controlling case law (e.g., 42 U.S.C. §§ 7604(a), 7413(e)(1); NRDC v. EPA, 749 F.3d 1055, 1062-64 (D.C. Cir. 2014)). Removal is not discretionary but required by law; the affirmative defense must be removed from the rules at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must follow prior petitions, reconsideration grants, and consent decrees
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is legally obligated by its 2014 grant of a rulemaking petition (Sierra Club) and by ongoing reconsideration processes and court-ordered consent decrees to address and remove the affirmative defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and implement prior agency commitments and court-ordered deadlines (e.g., Letter from Janet G. McCabe granting Sierra Club petition; 2012 petition/reconsideration materials; applicable consent decree provisions). Do not treat the issue as open-ended where prior grants/court action make it determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expeditious finalization required
rubrics_metrics.description: Because removal of the affirmative defense is legally required and determinative, EPA must 'expeditiously finalize its proposal' and finalize action very shortly after the close of the comment period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid undue delay; timing must account for the clear legal duty to act and any court-ordered deadlines. Final action should not be prolonged because the legal conclusion is straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove the affirmative defense across all rules containing it
rubrics_metrics.description: The affirmative defense sits separate from substantive emission standards and 'removing it requires no intensive or complex analysis for any source category'—the legal conclusion applies identically to all source categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should apply the same legal conclusion and remove the affirmative defense from all other EPA-promulgated rules that still contain it, not just the rules at issue in this proposed action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for environmental, public health, and environmental justice impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal of loopholes including affirmative defenses is 'expected to contribute to reduced excess emissions...and improve human and environmental health,' benefitting people of color, low-income populations, and Indigenous peoples; EPA's claim of 'no impacts' is disputable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and quantify air quality, health, and environmental justice impacts rather than dismissing them; include analysis showing how removal reduces excess emissions and benefits overburdened communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider enforcement and incentive effects of the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing loopholes and affirmative defenses 'takes away exemptions and defenses from liability that polluters routinely seek to invoke' and therefore makes standards easier to enforce and creates incentives to minimize excess emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how regulatory language (e.g., existence or removal of an affirmative defense) affects enforceability, compliance incentives, and real-world emissions behavior; include discussion of enforcement consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical evidence of excess emissions and affirmative defense usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical data (e.g., Texas reporting showing frequent, large emission events and high rates of affirmative-defense claims) and peer-reviewed studies linking excess emissions to health and EJ outcomes should inform conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support claims with concrete data and studies (examples cited: Hollingsworth et al., Health Consequences of Excess Emissions; Environmental Integrity Project & Environment Texas reports; studies on redlining and well siting). Do not rely solely on unsupported assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on 'bald claims' of no material impact without analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's statements that removal 'does not have a material impact on…the ability of Federal or State agencies to enforce standards' and that there will be 'no impacts on human health, the environment, and air quality' conflict with prior statements and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conclusory statements about lack of impacts; provide analysis and evidence when asserting no material impact. Where evidence indicates likely reductions in excess emissions, account for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unlawful or arbitrary regulatory outcomes in related rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: In related rulemakings, EPA should not pursue outcomes that would be 'unlawful and arbitrary,' such as reclassifying major sources as area sources through minor controls without a lawful basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure related regulatory actions have lawful and non-arbitrary legal and factual bases; flag and correct attempts to achieve regulatory goals by procedurally or substantively improper means.
